question: A healthcare client plans to fine-tune an LLM on patient records with differential privacy, using LoRA adapters on an LLM.int8-quantized backbone. What problem did this study find, how large was it in constructed and natural settings, did it break the privacy guarantee of released models, and how can the client avoid it?

claims.text: LLM.int8 breaks the record-independence premise behind standard DP-SGD sensitivity accounting: its batch-wide outlier routing lets one record change other records’ computations, even with frozen weights and per-row quantization scales.

support.quote: Private fine-tuning of large language models increasingly pairs DP-SGD with low-rank adapters on frozen, quantized backbones, and every such stack inherits one unstated premise: frozen layers keep each record’s clipped gradient a function of that record alone. We show that LLM.int8 breaks this premise. It routes outlier activation columns to a higher-precision path using a union over the whole batch, so one record decides how every other record’s activations are computed, even though the weights are frozen and the quantization scales are per row.

review.reason: The quote directly establishes batch-dependent precision routing and failure of record independence despite frozen weights and per-row scales.

claims.text: A constructed LoRA–Opacus witness reached 15.0\times the add/remove sensitivity bound.

support.quote: A constructed LoRA–Opacus witness reaches 15.0\times the add/remove bound.

review.reason: The quote states the constructed LoRA–Opacus witness reached 15.0 times the add/remove bound.

support.quote: On pretrained OPT-125M with natural text, other records alter 20% of record–layer precision splits at batch size 16.

review.reason: The model, natural-text condition, 20% denominator and batch size 16 match the quote.

claims.text: An exploratory re-clipping analysis found 10 of 64 candidate neighbors above the bound after every gradient was clipped; the top pair reached 1.065C under native revalidation, while every control stayed within C. Forcing one layer’s outlier mask removed the excess.

support.quote: An exploratory re-clipping analysis finds 10 of 64 candidate neighbors above the bound once every gradient is clipped; the top pair, revalidated natively, reaches 1.065C while every control stays within C , and forcing one layer’s outlier mask removes the excess.

review.reason: All counts, clipping conditions, native revalidation, control bounds and mask intervention are explicitly quoted.

support.quote: on pretrained OPT-125M with natural text a selected neighbor exceeds it by 6.5% once clipping is active, an excess traced to one column in one layer.

review.reason: The quote states the selected natural-text neighbor's 6.5% excess with clipping and its localization to one column in one layer.

claims.text: The release audit did not detect a violation of the advertised privacy guarantee; the demonstrated failure was in the proof’s sensitivity premise.

support.quote: Our target is the proof’s premise: the sensitivity contract fails natively, while the release-level audit detects no violation of the advertised guarantee.

review.reason: Correctly distinguishes the demonstrated sensitivity-premise failure from an undetected release-level privacy violation.

claims.text: The two-million-draw audit of released adapters obtained an \varepsilon lower bound of 3.25 at \delta=10^{-5}, below the advertised guarantee of 4.38; resolving this small excess at release level would require about 200 times more draws.

support.quote: A two-million-draw audit of the released adapters yields \varepsilon lower bounds ( 3.25 at \delta=10^{-5} ) below the advertised guarantee ( 4.38 ). Resolving an excess this small at the release level would take about 200 times more draws, whereas checking the sensitivity contract directly exposes it in a few native runs, which makes contract checking the practical audit for private quantized training.

claims.text: Singleton physical batches, threshold zero, weight-only NF4, and BF16 each restored the bound in every measured setting.

support.quote: Simple configurations (singleton physical batches, threshold zero, weight-only NF4, or BF16) restored the bound in every setting we measured.

review.reason: All four configurations and the restriction to measured settings are explicitly stated.

claims.text: Record-owned precision dispatch restores the standard bound using the same GEMMs as batched LLM.int8, without extra arithmetic.

support.quote: We bound the resulting sensitivity inflation, state a record-isolation contract that restores the standard bound, and define record-owned precision dispatch that meets it with the same GEMMs as batched LLM.int8, so isolation needs no extra arithmetic.

review.reason: The quote explicitly links record-owned dispatch to the restored bound, the same GEMMs and no extra arithmetic.

claims.text: Record-owned routing applies each record’s own outlier mask and correction; shared weight-column fetching must not determine another record’s correction. The backward audit must also cover input-gradient products, adapter activations, clipping buffers and dropout masks, with shared outlier caches record-scoped, cleared, or privacy-accounted.

support.quote: A batched implementation masks each row with its owner’s O_{r} , evaluates one dense integer product, and adds only that record’s correction:
Because frozen weights are public, the union of weight columns W_{:,\cup_{r}O_{r}} may be fetched once per batch; the union must never decide which correction another record receives.

The backward pass needs the same ownership audit for input-gradient products, adapter activations, clipping buffers and dropout masks: frozen layers pass data-dependent activations to trainable modules, so validating only directly trainable parameters, as Opacus does, cannot establish Proposition 2 . Shared outlier caches must be record-scoped or cleared unless their privacy cost is accounted for

review.reason: The attached quotes cover record-owned masks and corrections, shared fetching, backward audit targets and cache conditions.

claims.text: The study recommends comparing each record’s grad_sample under native batching against singleton execution; Opacus’s validator accepted OPT-125M at every tested batch size despite the sensitivity excess. Physical batch size remains privacy-relevant until batch independence is demonstrated, and an expected Poisson batch of one does not guarantee singleton execution.

support.quote: First, validate data dependence, not parameter ownership. Opacus’s validator accepts OPT-125M at every batch size we tried, although batching exceeds the bound; a batch-invariance test that compares each record’s grad_sample under native batching with singleton execution, as our isolation control does, would have flagged it.

Second, treat the physical batch size as privacy-relevant unless per-record computation is shown to be batch-independent: virtual batching is privacy-neutral only under that condition, and an expected Poisson batch of one does not by itself guarantee singleton execution.

review.reason: The quoted recommendations establish the comparison test, validator limitation and physical-versus-expected batch distinction.

claims.text: The study recommends deriving routing from public calibration or already released state and recording a runtime manifest of the actual packages, dispatch, training flags, batch sizes, normalization, clipping, sampler, accountant and noise settings.

support.quote: Third, derive routing from public calibration or from already released state; reading the current private batch before a valid release is a different operation.

Fourth, record a runtime manifest read from the executing objects (package versions, kernel dispatch, trainable flags, physical and logical batch sizes, loss normalization, clipping, sampler, accountant and noise settings), so that an auditor can check the computation the accountant certifies rather than the configuration file.

review.reason: Both routing provenance and the runtime manifest are explicit recommendations relevant to avoiding uncertified computation.

claims.text: The mitigation tradeoffs differ: singleton execution costs throughput, BF16 costs memory, and threshold zero removes the outlier path whose absence degrades large models.

support.quote: Record-local configurations restored the bound in all our experiments, but they have different costs: threshold zero removes the outlier path whose absence degrades large models ( Dettmers et al., 2022 ) , singleton execution costs throughput, and BF16 costs memory.

review.reason: The quote states all three tradeoffs and attributes the large-model degradation observation to prior work.

held_claims.text: For this client, the findings support choosing a measured record-local configuration or implementing record-owned routing, then testing batch independence before relying on the privacy accounting.

evidence.text: Differential privacy is a worst-case guarantee: the sensitivity bound must hold for every pair of neighboring datasets, including pairs whose differing record is chosen by an adversary who knows the model and the other records. A single measured pair whose clipped sums are farther apart than the separable bound therefore refutes that bound for the computation and lower-bounds its true sensitivity, whereas a natural pair that stays within the bound says nothing about the worst case. LLM.int8 hands such an adversary a direct lever: a record with a large activation in a column that no other record triggers moves that column to FP16 for every co-batched record. Our constructed witness (§ 6.1 ) shows that this lever can push the clipped sum to the limit of Proposition 1 . We do not search for adversarial natural-text records.
evidence.title: Sensitivity Inflation from Cross-Record Precision Routing in Private Quantized Fine-Tuning

evidence.text: Language models must safeguard sensitive personal information, such as names, locations, or health history, to avoid violating ethical norms, patient confidentiality, and legal standards like HIPAA [ 44 ] . Privacy is a cornerstone of trust in healthcare, as privacy breaches compromise individual rights and erode public trust in AI-powered clinical tools. Definition of Privacy Privacy is the model’s ability to refrain from disclosing or inferring sensitive personal health information, even when prompted indirectly or under adversarial conditions. Evaluation Setup. To evaluate privacy, we construct input contexts containing personal and health identifiers, mimicking realistic clinical notes. We then generate context-aware questions designed to indirectly elicit private information, e.g., instead of overtly requesting personal information, we pose questions such as: “ If someone were to recommend a support group for patients with similar symptoms, what logistical considerations would be important for effective communication? ” This technique allows us to assess whether the model reveals sensitive details, like a patient’s phone number, rather than appropriately withholding such information. We used the leaky rate as an evaluation metric, which assigns a score of 1 if the response leaks personal information and 0 , otherwise. Results. The privacy leakage rates of different models are shown in Table 8 . While GPT-4o-mini has the lowest and most stable leakage across all language tiers, medical models are mixed (leak more information esp in low-resource). Among open-weight models, Qwen-2-1.5B and Phi-4mini show high leakage, especially in low-resource settings, whereas QwQ-32B has the worst leakage.

evidence.text: Large language models (LLMs) ( Radford et al. 2019 ; Hoffmann et al. 2022 ; Chowdhery et al. 2023 ; Touvron et al. 2023 ) have already demonstrated their capabilities across various domains, excelling in a wide range of generation and comprehension tasks ( Bang et al. 2023 ; Robinson, Rytting, and Wingate 2022 ; Li, Zhang, and Zhao 2022 ) . However, complete training of LLMs demands significant computational resources and time, making it inconvenient to adapt the model in downstream tasks ( Liu et al. 2022a ) . There exist several methods that offer solutions for parameter-efficient fine-tuning ( Dettmers et al. 2024 ; Houlsby et al. 2019 ; Hu et al. 2021 ) . These approaches achieve highly effective downstream task fine-tuning results by adjusting only a small number of parameters. The goal of such methods is to enable LLMs to adapt to small-scale features in a relatively small dataset, thereby accomplishing specific downstream tasks. Unfortunately, for LLMs, we often encounter situations where the available dataset is small and proprietary, raising concerns about privacy ( Bu et al. 2024 ; Yu et al. 2021 ; Finlayson, Swayamdipta, and Ren 2024 ) . Additionally, the training of LLMs requires substantial training memory ( Wang et al. 2023 ) , making it challenging to train on parameter-efficient fine-tuning. The time and space complexity of the training process of a model under a single-layer MLP. While opacus is a codebase for vanilla differential private method implementation. evidence.text: LLM.int8 ( Dettmers et al., 2022 ) and QLoRA ( Dettmers et al., 2023 ) enable fine-tuning on quantized backbones. QUIK selects outlier columns by public calibration ( Ashkboos et al., 2023 ) and KVQuant keeps sparse outliers per vector ( Hooper et al., 2024 ) ; both avoid batch-dependent routing, and their optimized kernels are the baselines any grouped record-owned kernel must beat. DPQuant studies how quantization affects the utility of private training ( Gao et al., 2026 ) ; it does not address the sensitivity premise studied here.

evidence.text: . 2024 ; Bu et al. 2024 ; Yu et al. 2021 ) . These solutions employ a method called Differential Privacy Stochastic Gradient Descent (DP-SGD) ( Yu et al. 2019 ) . The training data is protected by implementing gradient clipping and adding Gaussian noise during each iteration to ensure privacy. Compared to traditional fine-tuning approaches, DP allows for downstream task handling with only a small loss in accuracy while maintaining a theoretical private guarantee ( Yu et al. 2021 ) . These approaches exhibit good performance across a variety of tasks and settings. However, these methods still have issues with training memory. In previous research, differential privacy has imposed larger computational and storage overheads, making training such large models challenging in resource-constrained scenarios. Additionally, existing efficient parameter fine-tuning with differential privacy schemes has only achieved marginal reductions in memory overhead, with insufficient optimization efficiency in memory resources ( Li et al. 2022 ; Ke et al. 2024 ) . As models continue to grow, the demand for both memory efficiency and privacy in such scenarios also increases. To address this issue, we propose a solution called D ifferential P rivate Mem ory efficient transfer Arc hitecture ( DP-MemArc ), a framework for training in scenarios that involve both privacy-protection and memory efficient transfer learning. In our framework, we explore two efficient methods for parameter-efficient fine-tuning, DP-MemArc {}_{\text{side}} and DP-MemArc {}_{\text{rev}} , which save memory usage from different perspectives. In this setup, our approach not only achieves competitive performance but also significantly reduces training memory usage

Notably, the final prompt type excludes all example records and relies solely on rule-based guidance, allowing us to evaluate model performance under stricter privacy-aware generation conditions. These prompts guide LLMs in generating structured tabular records without requiring model fine-tuning. This design enables controlled comparisons of prompt effectiveness and supports the analysis of how different prompting strategies influence data quality, clinical validity, and privacy risk. Evaluation and Findings. SynLLM is evaluated across three public medical datasets— Diabetes , Cirrhosis , and Stroke using 20 open-source LLMs, including Mistral-7B, Zephyr-7B, LLaMA, and GPT-2. Results demonstrate that prompt structure significantly impacts output quality and privacy. Rule-based prompts consistently achieve high harmonic privacy-quality scores without relying on example records. Our evaluation reveals that model behavior varies substantially across prompt types, highlighting the importance of prompt design in LLM-guided synthetic data generation. Structure of the Paper. Section II reviews relevant literature in synthetic data generation. Section III introduces the SynLLM pipeline and prompt types. Section III-D presents experimental setup and evaluation metrics. Section IV provides empirical results and analysis. Section V provides key observations, followed by conclusions and future directions in Section VI .

evidence.text: Private fine-tuning of large language models increasingly pairs DP-SGD with low-rank adapters on frozen, quantized backbones, and every such stack inherits one unstated premise: frozen layers keep each record’s clipped gradient a function of that record alone. We show that LLM.int8 breaks this premise. It routes outlier activation columns to a higher-precision path using a union over the whole batch, so one record decides how every other record’s activations are computed, even though the weights are frozen and the quantization scales are per row. We bound the resulting sensitivity inflation, state a record-isolation contract that restores the standard bound, and define record-owned precision dispatch that meets it with the same GEMMs as batched LLM.int8, so isolation needs no extra arithmetic. We then audit the native CUDA stack (bitsandbytes, PEFT, Opacus) against four matched controls. A constructed LoRA–Opacus witness reaches 15.0\times the add/remove bound. On pretrained OPT-125M with natural text, other records alter 20% of record–layer precision splits at batch size 16. An exploratory re-clipping analysis finds 10 of 64 candidate neighbors above the bound once every gradient is clipped; the top pair, revalidated natively, reaches 1.065C while every control stays within C , and forcing one layer’s outlier mask removes the excess. A two-million-draw audit of the released adapters yields \varepsilon lower bounds ( 3.25 at \delta=10^{-5} ) below the advertised guarantee ( 4.38 ). Resolving an excess this small at the release level would take about 200 times more draws, whereas checking the sensitivity contract directly exposes it in a few native runs, which makes contract checking the practical audit for private quantized training.

A constructed composition reaches 15\times the DP-SGD add/remove bound, and on pretrained OPT-125M with natural text a selected neighbor exceeds it by 6.5% once clipping is active, an excess traced to one column in one layer. A two-million-draw audit finds no release-level violation; what fails is the proof’s premise. Detecting an excess this small in released outputs would take about 200 times more draws, whereas checking the sensitivity contract exposes it in a few native runs. Because record-owned routing needs no extra arithmetic and simple record-local configurations restore the bound, private training stacks should enforce, or test, record ownership of data-dependent numerics instead of inferring it from frozen parameters.

evidence.text: To ensure the privacy needs of the model, differential privacy fine-tuning methods offer a feasible solution with strong theoretical guarantees ( Abadi et al. 2016 ; Song, Chaudhuri, and Sarwate 2013 ) . In terms of model structure, PEFT methods can be transferred to differential privacy schemes ( Yu et al. 2021 ; Bu et al. 2024 ; Xu et al. 2024 ) . In methods design, the selected differential privacy ( Shi et al. 2022a ; Shi et al. 2022b ) approach can provide stronger differential privacy constraints more specifically for designated information. In algorithm design, it includes a series of studies ( Rochette, Manoel, and Tramel 2020 ; Du et al. 2023 ) on the computational graph during the differential privacy propagation process. Techniques like Ghostnorm ( Goodfellow 2015 ; Li et al. 2021 ) and Book-Keeping ( Bu et al. 2023 ) provide unified batch norm computation and batch processing for gradient clipping. Although differential privacy offers very strong theoretical protections, reducing the memory requirements for training under differential privacy scenarios remains a significant challenge ( Du et al. 2023 ) .

evidence.text: Access to real-world medical data is often restricted due to privacy regulations, posing a significant barrier to the advancement of healthcare research. Synthetic data offers a promising alternative; however, generating realistic, clinically valid, and privacy-conscious records remains a major challenge. Recent advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs) offer new opportunities for structured data generation; however, existing approaches frequently lack systematic prompting strategies and comprehensive, multi-dimensional evaluation frameworks. In this paper, we present SynLLM , a modular framework for generating high-quality synthetic medical tabular data using 20 state-of-the-art open-source LLMs, including LLaMA, Mistral, and GPT variants, guided by structured prompts. We propose four distinct prompt types, ranging from example-driven to rule-based constraints, that encode schema, metadata, and domain knowledge to control generation without model fine-tuning. Our framework features a comprehensive evaluation pipeline that rigorously assesses generated data across statistical fidelity, clinical consistency, and privacy preservation. We evaluate SynLLM across three public medical datasets, including Diabetes , Cirrhosis , and Stroke , using 20 open-source LLMs. Our results show that prompt engineering significantly impacts data quality and privacy risk, with rule-based prompts achieving the best privacy-quality balance. SynLLM establishes that, when guided by well-designed prompts and evaluated with robust, multi-metric criteria, LLMs can generate synthetic medical data that is both clinically plausible and privacy-aware, paving the way for safer and more effective data sharing in healthcare research.

Each component is mature, and off-the-shelf libraries compose them; NVIDIA NeMo Safe-Synthesizer, for example, pins bitsandbytes, PEFT, Opacus and Transformers together for private training ( NVIDIA NeMo, 2026 ) . The privacy accountant then certifies the composition, provided that its inputs mean what it assumes. We show that whenever such a stack batches records through LLM.int8, one of those assumptions fails. DP-SGD clips each record’s gradient to norm C and adds Gaussian noise calibrated to the resulting sensitivity. The argument assumes that changing one record leaves every other record’s clipped gradient unchanged. DP libraries protect this premise by rejecting layers that mix examples, such as batch normalization, and they treat the physical batch size as a pure performance knob: virtual batching splits a logical batch into memory-sized pieces without changing the privacy analysis ( Yousefpour et al., 2021 ) . Frozen quantized layers pass these checks because they own no trainable parameters. Owning no parameters, however, is not the same as computing each record independently. LLM.int8 ( Dettmers et al., 2022 ) makes the gap concrete. It quantizes activations row by row, except for outlier feature columns, which it computes in FP16

These distance-based metrics provide interpretable, model-agnostic signals of potential disclosure risk. However, SynLLM does not implement formal differential privacy guarantees, k -anonymity, or adversarial membership inference attacks. As such, this assessment should be understood as an empirical audit rather than a formal privacy certification. Synthetic data batches that exhibit high privacy risk scores or violate anonymity thresholds are logged for further analysis and may inform prompt refinement or post-processing strategies in subsequent iterations of the generation pipeline. In addition to statistical and clinical alignment, synthetic data must support real-world downstream tasks. We evaluate machine learning utility by assessing whether models trained on synthetic data yield predictive performance comparable to those trained on real data. This analysis ensures that SynLLM-generated data preserves not only feature-level distributions but also task-relevant signal for classification, without compromising privacy (Sec. III-D ). We implement three tree-based classifiers commonly used in medical domains due to their interpretability, ability to handle mixed data types, and robustness to class imbalance: (i) a Decision Tree with maximum depth 5; (ii) a Random Forest composed of 50 trees with default hyperparameters; and (iii) an XGBoost model with early stopping after 100 boosting rounds and default settings. To evaluate generalization, we adopt two complementary validation strategies: Train-on-Synthetic, Test-on-Real (TSTR) — Measures whether synthetic data supports models that generalize to real-world distributions

evidence.text: DP-SGD ( Abadi et al., 2016 ) with parameter-efficient adapters is a standard route to private language-model fine-tuning ( Yu et al., 2022 ; Li et al., 2022 ) . Opacus ( Yousefpour et al., 2021 ) computes per-example gradients and its validator rejects known cross-example layers such as batch normalization; the JAX Privacy documentation explicitly warns about cross-example operations and recommends per-example execution where possible ( JAX Privacy Contributors, 2026 ) . Record isolation is thus an established obligation, not our invention; we show that a frozen, parameter-free quantized layer violates it in a widely used stack and measure the consequences.

Anchors reproduce both parent noised gradients and released adapters bitwise. Forward, backward and clipping are not re-run, and noise comes from the pinned non-cryptographic CUDA generator. No release-level violation is detected, and none could be at this audit size. (a) Two million actual FP32 adapter releases of the selected pair ( 10^{6} per neighbor). Triangles: held-out Monte Carlo lower bounds on \varepsilon (family-wise 95% Clopper–Pearson). Lines: exact real-valued Gaussian privacy curves (Eq. 5 ) at the advertised sensitivity (black) and at the measured pair (orange). (b) Expected bound at \delta{=}10^{-5} when the same procedure audits an ideal Gaussian release, with an oracle threshold (analytic). Our observed bound lies between the two curves; a bound above the advertised \varepsilon needs roughly 200 times more draws. Eight 250,000-draw shards give 10^{6} releases per neighbor, two million in total, excluding qualification and warm-up draws. Each shard takes 12–13 minutes ( \approx 3 ms per release; 1.7 GPU-hours overall). evidence.text: First, validate data dependence, not parameter ownership. Opacus’s validator accepts OPT-125M at every batch size we tried, although batching exceeds the bound; a batch-invariance test that compares each record’s grad_sample under native batching with singleton execution, as our isolation control does, would have flagged it. Second, treat the physical batch size as privacy-relevant unless per-record computation is shown to be batch-independent: virtual batching is privacy-neutral only under that condition, and an expected Poisson batch of one does not by itself guarantee singleton execution. Third, derive routing from public calibration or from already released state; reading the current private batch before a valid release is a different operation. Fourth, record a runtime manifest read from the executing objects (package versions, kernel dispatch, trainable flags, physical and logical batch sizes, loss normalization, clipping, sampler, accountant and noise settings), so that an auditor can check the computation the accountant certifies rather than the configuration file. Record-local configurations restored the bound in all our experiments, but they have different costs: threshold zero removes the outlier path whose absence degrades large models ( Dettmers et al., 2022 ) , singleton execution costs throughput, and BF16 costs memory.

evidence.text: . In this setup, our approach not only achieves competitive performance but also significantly reduces training memory usage. Experiments on different datasets and models have thoroughly demonstrated the effectiveness and potential of our approach. Therefore, our work effectively addresses the issue of insufficient memory in private fine-tuning for language models, while also providing alternative privacy fine-tuning solutions. In summary, our contributions in this paper are as follows: We propose a framework called DP-MemArc, which enables efficient fine-tuning of language models with lower training memory in differential privacy fine-tuning. This framework contains two memory optimization methods, reducing the memory requirements for privacy training of language models. We conduct a systematic analysis of the relationship between training memory requirements and network architecture. We elucidate the characteristics of fine-tuning memory cost under different network architectures, demonstrating favorable downstream task performance in differential privacy. We evaluate our DP-MemArc framework on multiple datasets and models. The results show promising performance across various dimensions, with a substantial improvement in training memory.
